items.text: **Mnemonic: Rule of 12:** Any nucleus that is inclusive of 12 is medial. It includes nuclei III, IV, VI and XII. The rest are lateral.
**Rule of M:** 3 primary medial tracts of the Brainstem. Includes Motor Tract (Corticospinal Tract), Medial Lemniscus and Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus.
**Rule of S:** Lateral or “side” tracts. Includes Spinothalamic tract, Sympathetic tract and spinocerebellar tracts.

**Anterior Spinal Artery:** Its occlusion leads to medial medullary syndrome, resulting in contralateral hemiplegia, loss of vibration and position sense, and tongue paralysis on the same side.
**AICA (Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery):** Occlusion leads to lateral pontine syndrome, causing symptoms like facial paralysis, vertigo, nystagmus, and ataxia.
Medial Medullary Syndrome (Dejerine Syndrome)

items.text: **Cause:** Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery
**Features:**
**Contralateral Hemiplegia:** Due to damage to the medullary pyramid.
**Loss of Vibration and Position Sense:** Resulting from damage to the medial lemniscus.
**Tongue Paralysis (Same Side):** Caused by injury to the hypoglossal (XII) cranial nerve.

blocks.text: Lateral Inferior Pontine Syndrome

items.text: **Cause:** Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)
**On Side of Lesion:**
Nystagmus, Vertigo, Nausea, Vomiting, Oscillopsia: Due to vestibular nerve/nucleus involvement.
Facial Paralysis
Impaired Conjugate Gaze: Involvement of the center for lateral gaze.
Deafness and Tinnitus: Related to the auditory nerve or cochlear nucleus.
Ataxia: Affecting the middle cerebellar peduncle and cerebellar hemisphere.
Impaired Sensation Over Face: Due to involvement of the descending tract and nucleus of the fifth nerve.
**On Side Opposite Lesion:**
Impaired Pain and Thermal Sensation: Involving the spinothalamic tract over one-half of the body, which may include the face.

blocks.text: **Anterior cerebral artery, PICA (Option A):** Anterior Cerebral Artery: Occlusion affects the medial frontal and parietal lobes, causing contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, but does not cause the medial medullary syndrome. PICA: Occlusion leads to lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome), not lateral pontine syndrome.

**Posterior cerebral artery, Basilar artery (Option B):** Posterior Cerebral Artery: Occlusion affects the occipital lobe, causing visual field deficits and sensory disturbances, but not medial medullary syndrome. Basilar Artery: Occlusion leads to various brainstem syndromes, but is not specifically linked to lateral pontine syndrome.

**Vertebral artery, Superior cerebellar artery (Option D):** Vertebral Artery: Occlusion affects posterior circulation, causing various syndromes, but not medial medullary syndrome. Superior Cerebellar Artery: Occlusion primarily impacts the cerebellum and brainstem, but does not cause lateral pontine syndrome.

blocks.text: The nucleus of the solitary tract receives general visceral afferent sensations from the carotid body and carotid sinus primarily through the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX). The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) carries sensory information from the carotid body (chemoreceptor) and carotid sinus (baroreceptor) to the nucleus of the solitary tract, which is involved in regulating blood pressure and respiratory responses.
Nucleus of Tractus Solitarius
It is a composite nucleus located in the medulla. Its functions are:

items.text: **General Visceral Afferent (Lower Part):** Receives visceral sensations.
**Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX):** From tonsil, pharynx, posterior tongue, carotid body, and carotid sinus.
**Vagus nerve (X):** From the pharynx, larynx, trachea, oesophagus, and thoracic/abdominal viscera. (Option A ruled out)
**Special Visceral Afferent (Upper Part):** Receives taste sensations.
**Facial nerve (VII):** Anterior two-thirds of tongue and palate (except circumvallate papillae). (Option B ruled out)
**The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX):** Posterior one-third of the tongue, including circumvallate papillae.
**Vagus nerve (X):** Posterior tongue and epiglottis.

blocks.text: **Special somatic efferent; Trigeminal nerve (Option D):** Special somatic efferent fibers are related to the motor innervation of certain muscles, while the trigeminal nerve (CN V) primarily carries sensory information (touch, pain) from the face and does not innervate the carotid body or sinus.

The jaw jerk reflex is a deep tendon reflex with supraspinal involvement which is initiated by tapping the jaw. Masseter reflex or Jaw jerk reflex It is a deep tendon reflex. The reflex is initiated by tapping the midline of the mandible, which rapidly stretches the jaw-closing muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid). The stretch activates muscle spindle afferents, which are sensory receptors in the muscles.

items.text: **Afferent pathway:** Muscle spindle afferents → Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
**Integration centre (Relay):** Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option B ruled out)
**Efferent pathway:** Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve → Mandibular nerve. (Option C ruled out)

blocks.text: This results in the contraction of these jaw-closing muscles and finally closure of the jaw.

The jaw jerk reflex is the only significant supraspinal monosynaptic reflex due to its relay in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option D ruled out) The jaw jerk reflex can be tested in neurological examinations to assess the integrity of the trigeminal nerve and the brainstem pathways.
Mesencephalic Nucleus is located around the cerebral aqueduct and carries proprioceptive impulses from the muscles of mastication, facial, and extraocular muscles.
The trigeminal nerve has four nuclei as follows:

items.text: **Main Sensory Nucleus** Located in the posterior part of the pons, lateral to the motor nucleus. Continuous below with the spinal nucleus.
**Spinal Nucleus** Extends from the pons to the second cervical segment of the spinal cord. Receives sensations of pain and temperature. (Option B ruled out)
**Mesencephalic Nucleus** Located in the lateral part of the grey matter around the cerebral aqueduct. Receives proprioceptive impulses from muscles of mastication, facial, and extraocular muscles.

**Motor Nucleus** Located in the pons, medial to the main sensory nucleus. Controls muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric. (Option D ruled out)

blocks.text: Sensory component of Trigeminal Nuclei The motor component of Trigeminal Nuclei Carries pain, temperature, touch, pressure, and proprioception from the face. Main sensory nucleus - touch and pressure. (Option A ruled out) Spinal nucleus - pain and temperature. It extends till C2 of the spinal cord.

Mesencephalic nucleus - proprioception. The motor nucleus receives inputs from both cerebral hemispheres, the reticular formation, and the red nucleus and forms a reflex arc with the mesencephalic nucleus. Supplies muscles of mastication- Temporalis Masseter Lateral pterygoid Medial pterygoid Other muscles like Tensor tympani Tensor veli palatini Mylohyoid Anterior belly of digastric
Damage to the trochlear nucleus causes difficulty in downward and lateral gaze, often resulting in a compensatory head tilt to the opposite side.

items.text: **Oculomotor Nucleus (CN III):** (Option A ruled out) The eye cannot move upward, downward, or inward. At rest, the eye is in a down-and-out position. The patient experiences double vision (diplopia). The upper eyelid droops (ptosis) from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris. The pupil is widely dilated and nonreactive to light due to paralysis of the sphincter pupillae and unopposed sympathetic dilator activity. Accommodation is impaired.
**Trochlear Nucleus (CN IV):** Difficulty in downward and lateral gaze. Patients may exhibit a compensatory head tilt to the opposite side to manage diplopia (double vision).
**Abducens Nucleus (CN VI):** Medial strabismus (the affected eye cannot abduct), leading to horizontal diplopia. The affected eye is often turned inward. Diplopia is also seen. (Option C ruled out)

**Hypoglossal Nucleus (CN XII):** Weakness of the tongue on the side of the lesion, causing atrophy and fasciculations. On protrusion, the tongue may deviate toward the affected side. (Option D ruled out)

blocks.text: The patient is diagnosed with Wallenberg Syndrome due to the presence of ipsilateral loss of temperature sensation on the face, contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the trunk, difficulty swallowing, ipsilateral ataxia, and giddiness. The spinal nucleus and tract of the trigeminal nerve are responsible for the ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face, which is a hallmark feature of Wallenberg Syndrome.
Wallenberg Syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome)

Due to stroke or infarction in the lateral part of the medulla oblongata. Mainly due to occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), a branch of the vertebral artery. Sometimes the vertebral artery directly supplies the lateral brainstem. Affects the dorsolateral aspect of the medulla and the inferior surface of the cerebellum.
Anatomical structure affected and features:

items.text: **Spinothalamic tract:** Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation of the trunk. (Option A ruled out)
**Spinal nucleus and tract of the trigeminal nerve:** Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation of the face.
**Nucleus ambiguus:** Ipsilateral paralysis of muscles of the palate, pharynx, and larynx.
**Inferior cerebellar peduncle and cerebellum:** Ipsilateral ataxia. (Option C ruled out)
**Vestibular nuclei:** Giddiness. (Option D ruled out)

blocks.text: **Lesion is in the oculomotor nerve fascicles and corticospinal fibers (Option A):** Correct because Weber syndrome involves a midbrain lesion affecting the corticospinal tract and the oculomotor nerve fascicles.
**Hemiplegia is present on the opposite side of the lesion (Option B):** Correct because corticospinal fibers before decussation are damaged, causing contralateral hemiplegia.
**There is a lateral squint on the same side of the lesion (Option C):** Correct because oculomotor nerve palsy causes the eye to deviate laterally on the ipsilateral side.
**None of the above (Option D):** Correct answer since no statements are incorrect.

At the level of the motor decussation, corticospinal fibres cross from the anterior funiculi to the contralateral side, a hallmark of this level.
Internal Organization of the Medulla Oblongata
1. Transverse Section at Motor (Pyramidal) Decussation Level
The inferior medulla adapts to accommodate brainstem nuclei and fibres.
Corticospinal fibres cross at the motor decussation, decreasing the pyramid size. (Option B)
Ventral grey column divides into:

items.text: Supraspinal nucleus (first cervical nerve origin, continuous with the hypoglossal nerve nucleus).
Nucleus of the accessory nerve (aligned with the nucleus ambiguus).

blocks.text: Surrounding tracts:

items.text: Ventral corticospinal tract (medioventral).
Ventral and dorsal spinocerebellar tracts (dorsolateral).

blocks.text: Dorsal grey column modified by the presence of the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus, continuous with spinal structures.
2. Transverse Section at Sensory Decussation (Dorsal Column–Medial Lemniscus System)
Nuclei and tracts present: Nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus, receiving first-order afferent fibres.
Second-order axons (internal arcuate fibres) cross the midline as sensory decussation to form the medial lemniscus. (Option A ruled out)
Medial lemniscus: Located dorsal to the pyramid. Inferior olivary complex appears lateral to it. (Option D ruled out)
Other key structures: Dorsal spinocerebellar and trigeminal nerve tracts, reticular formation, corticospinal tract, medial longitudinal fasciculus, and tectospinal tract.
3. Transverse Section at Caudal End of Fourth Ventricle
Grey matter increases due to nuclei associated with cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and VIII.
Key nuclei:

items.text: Inferior olivary complex.
Hypoglossal nucleus, vagus dorsal motor nucleus, salivatory nuclei, nucleus solitarius, and vestibular nuclei. (Option C ruled out)

blocks.text: Restiform body forms the dorsal lateral border, carrying afferent fibers (spinocerebellar and olivocerebellar tracts).
Other structures: Spinal trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, reticular formation. Spinocerebellar, spinothalamic, and rubrospinal tracts ventral to the olivary complex and pyramid.

rows: Glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), cranial accessory (XIcr) and hypoglossal (XII)

blocks.text: A lesion affecting the interpeduncular fossa could damage the oculomotor nerve (CN III), which emerges from this region, leading to diplopia and ptosis.
**Interpeduncular fossa** It is a deep depression of the ventral surface of the midbrain between the two crura cerebri.
The lateral wall of the interpeduncular fossa bears the oculomotor sulcus, from which rootlets of the oculomotor nerve emerge from the brainstem and aggregate into a single fascicle. (Option C)
